title: Joy in Chains
subtitle: Philippians in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
Paul wrote Philippians from under guard, and it is the most joyful letter he ever sent.

This book walks through its four chapters in twenty-four short poems. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture, so you can read the whole thing in an evening, or one page a morning.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the letter itself alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Joy in Chains
parts.epigraph: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
parts.lightHint: Near 'the first day' (Philippians 1:3) in Part 1: Joy in Chains

parts.title: The Way Down
parts.epigraph: but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant
parts.lightHint: Near 'the pulled-out chair' (Philippians 2:3–4) in Part 2: The Way Down

parts.title: Pressing On
parts.epigraph: I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

parts.title: Peace on Guard
parts.epigraph: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
parts.lightHint: Near 'two names' (Philippians 4:2–3) in Part 4: Peace on Guard

paintings.title: the first day
paintings.epigraph: “I thank my God whenever I remember you”
paintings.poem:
it started by a river
outside the city gate—
a few women, a Sabbath,
a stranger with a story.

a seller of purple cloth
opened her heart
before she opened her door.

that is how a church begins:
not with a building
but with a table set
for someone passing through.

and years later,
in chains, far away,
he still remembers
the first day.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Philippians 1:3, grace meets us right beside the moving water: how does the closing thought—“and years later, in chains, far away, he still remembers the first day”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: unfinished
paintings.epigraph: “he who began a good work in you will complete it”
paintings.poem:
the potter does not leave
a bowl half-turned on the wheel
and walk away.

you are not
the abandoned project,
the draft in the drawer,
the garden gone to seed.

his hands are still wet.
the wheel is still turning.

what he started in you
he means to finish.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “unfinished” (Philippians 1:6) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“what he started in you he means to finish”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: the heaviest thing
paintings.epigraph: “I have you in my heart”
paintings.poem:
iron on his wrists,
a guard at his shoulder,
a lamp burning low—

and still
the heaviest thing he carries
is love.

he writes your names
the way other men
count coins.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Philippians 1:7)—where in your own home or work today does “he writes your names the way other men count coins” ring true?

paintings.title: the palace guard
paintings.epigraph: “it became evident to the whole palace guard”
paintings.poem:
they chained a soldier to him,
and then another,
and another,
thinking they had him held.

but a man chained to Paul
has nowhere to go
but listen.

one by one
the guards went home
with more than they came with.

what was meant to stop the message
became the room
where it was told.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “what was meant to stop the message became the room where it was told.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: whose hand
paintings.epigraph: “Christ is proclaimed. I rejoice in this, yes, and will rejoice.”
paintings.poem:
some sowed out of envy,
some out of love.
the soil did not ask
whose hand had thrown the seed.

he could have kept score.
he chose to keep rejoicing.

there is a freedom
in caring more
that the name is spoken
than who gets credit
for speaking it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “some sowed out of envy, some out of love.” Looking through the lens of Philippians 1:18, what does it mean to discover that “there is a freedom in caring more that the name is spoken than who gets credit for speaking it”?

paintings.title: two doors
paintings.epigraph: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”
paintings.poem:
he stood between two doors—

one opening home,
one opening back onto the work.

stay, and there is fruit.
go, and there is Christ.

either way, he is held.

what can you take
from a man
who has already
been given everything?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the open threshold in this painting (Philippians 1:21–23)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: the pulled-out chair
paintings.epigraph: “each counting others better than himself”
paintings.poem:
humility is small work:
pulling out the chair
before you sit,
noticing who hasn't eaten,
letting the other story
be the one that's told.

it is a turning of the head—
away from the mirror,
toward the window.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the open window facing home: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “it is a turning of the head— away from the mirror, toward the window”?

paintings.title: the way down
paintings.epigraph: “but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”
paintings.poem:
every other god
climbed.

this one
came down the stairs—
past the throne,
past the crown,
past the dignity of distance,

down to the basin,
down to the towel,
down to the dust on our feet,

down further still,
to a wooden cross
on a hill outside the wall.

the way to know him
is the same way down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “the way down” (Philippians 2:6–8) from “every other god climbed” to “the way to know him is the same way down”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: the field bows
paintings.epigraph: “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow”
paintings.poem:
the wind moves across the wheat
and the whole field bows
at once.

no one told it to.
it simply knows
where the wind is coming from.

one day
every knee—
in heaven, on earth,
and under it—

the proud, the tired,
the ones who never believed
it would come to this—

and every tongue
will say his name
the way the field says wind.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “the field bows” (Philippians 2:10–11) arrives at: “one day every knee— in heaven, on earth, and under it— the proud, the tired, the ones who never believed it would come to this— and every tongue will say his name the way the field says wind.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: one window
paintings.epigraph: “you are seen as lights in the world”
paintings.poem:
you don't have to be a lighthouse.

a lamp in one window
on one dark street
is enough
for whoever is walking home
tonight.

so put down the complaint.
let the argument go cold.
tend the small flame.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Philippians 2:14–15: “let the argument go cold. tend the small flame”?

paintings.title: poured out
paintings.epigraph: “if I am poured out on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice”
paintings.poem:
some lives are kept
like good wine in a cellar,
sealed and safe.

his was poured—
all of it,
over the offering
of other people's faith.

he did not call it waste.
he called it joy,
and asked us
to rejoice with him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the quiet centerpiece of “poured out”: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “he called it joy, and asked us to rejoice with him”?

paintings.title: sorrow on sorrow
paintings.epigraph: “God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but on me also”
paintings.poem:
Epaphroditus came with a gift
and nearly didn't make it home.

fever in a foreign city.
a friend at his bedside
bracing for grief
on top of grief.

and then—mercy.
the fever broke.

sometimes the miracle
is not a sea split open
but a man sitting up in bed,
asking for bread.

and the friend who waited
was healed too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “and the friend who waited was healed too.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Philippians 2:27 right now?

paintings.title: credentials
paintings.epigraph: “I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ”
paintings.poem:
eighth-day circumcised.
tribe of Benjamin.
Hebrew of Hebrews.
Pharisee. zealot. blameless.

he had the ré sumé
every room respected.

then he met the One
who didn't need it—

and folded it up
like an old receipt,
and let it go.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Philippians 3:5–7, grace meets us right beside the quiet centerpiece of “credentials”: how does the closing thought—“then he met the One who didn't need it— and folded it up like an old receipt, and let it go”—steady your footing for the road ahead?

paintings.title: the trade
paintings.epigraph: “I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus”
paintings.poem:
a man sells everything
for a single field.
the neighbors call it foolish
until they see the treasure.

this is that trade:
all my own shine
for his righteousness,
all my trying
for his gift.

I would not trade back.
not for the world.
not for the whole of it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If today’s painting of “the trade” (Philippians 3:8–9) hung beside the door you walk out of this morning, how would its final line—“I would not trade back. not for the whole of it”—shape your choices?

paintings.title: to know him
paintings.epigraph: “that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection”
paintings.poem:
not to know about him.
to know him—

the way you know
a voice in the dark,
the way you know
a hand on your shoulder.

to know the power
that rolled the stone,
and the fellowship
of the wounds that came first.

there is no Easter morning
that does not pass
through Friday.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Every stop on the Pilgrim Walk shows how God meets us in ordinary places (Philippians 3:10)—where in your own home or work today does “there is no Easter morning that does not pass through Friday” ring true?

paintings.title: taken hold of
paintings.epigraph: “I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus”
paintings.poem:
I have not arrived.
I will not pretend I have.

but here is the good news
hidden in the middle of the sentence:

I reach for him
because he already
reached for me.

my grip is weak.
his is not.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Take a slow breath and read the final line again: “my grip is weak. his is not.” How would you walk through the next hour differently if you carried that truth with you?

paintings.title: one thing
paintings.epigraph: “forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before”
paintings.poem:
the runner does not look back
at the stadium dust
or count the stumbles.

eyes forward.
arms open.
lungs burning.

the old failures,
the old trophies—
both left behind
on the same track.

one thing.
the upward call.
the finish
where he stands waiting.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of a season when you knew the feeling of “the runner does not look back at the stadium dust or count the stumbles.” Looking through the lens of Philippians 3:13–14, what does it mean to discover that “the finish where he stands waiting”?

paintings.title: citizens
paintings.epigraph: “For our citizenship is in heaven”
paintings.poem:
Philippi was proud
to be a little Rome—
Roman roads, Roman law,
Roman names on the gate.

he wrote them:
you belong to a different city.

so live like foreigners
who love the place they're in
but keep one eye
on the eastern road,

waiting for the King
to come home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look closely at the city gate in this painting (Philippians 3:20)—if you could leave one anxious weight beside it today, what would you set down?

paintings.title: two names
paintings.epigraph: “whose names are in the book of life”
paintings.poem:
Euodia. Syntyche.
two women who once worked side by side
now cannot share a room.

he doesn't pick a side.
he calls them both by name,
and reminds them
where their names are written.

hard to hold a grudge
against someone
on the same page
of the book of life.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Let your eyes rest on the brushwork and light around the name by which He calls you: what quiet prayer rises in you when you read, “hard to hold a grudge against someone on the same page of the book of life”?

paintings.title: twice
paintings.epigraph: “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!””
paintings.poem:
he said it twice
because he knew
we would not believe it
the first time.

written from a cell.
not after the release—
before it.

joy is not the weather.
it is the sky
behind the weather.

rejoice.
I'll say it again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Linger with the movement in “twice” (Philippians 4:4) from “he said it twice because he knew we would not believe it the first time” to “rejoice. I'll say it again”—where do you find yourself along that arc today?

paintings.title: the sentry
paintings.epigraph: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts”
paintings.poem:
Philippi knew soldiers—
the sound of boots at the gate,
the watch changed at night.

so he borrowed their word:
peace will stand guard.

not the absence of trouble,
but a sentry at the door of your heart,
awake while you sleep.

so tell him everything.
the whole list.
say thank you somewhere in it.
then lie down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Notice how “the sentry” (Philippians 4:6–7) arrives at: “say thank you somewhere in it. then lie down.” Who in your life is walking a hard stretch of road today and needs you to share this grace with them?

paintings.title: the walls of the mind
paintings.epigraph: “whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report”
paintings.poem:
the mind is a room.
you decide
what hangs on the walls.

so hang the true things—
the honest, the just,
the clean, the kind,

a child's laugh,
bread from the oven,
the last light on the hills.

think about these.
let them furnish you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What if the most important thing you remember before tonight is the quiet lesson of Philippians 4:8: “think about these. let them furnish you”?

paintings.title: the secret
paintings.epigraph: “I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry”
paintings.poem:
the verse on the gym wall
was first written
by a hungry man.

I can do all things—
be full,
go without,
sleep under guard,
eat from a borrowed bowl—

not because I am strong,
but because he is,
and he is here
in the plenty
and the lack.

that is the secret:
not more,
but him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Imagine standing inside this frame beside the stones of the wall: what hurry or noise in your week begins to fade when you hear, “that is the secret: not more, but him”?

paintings.title: fragrance
paintings.epigraph: “a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to God”
paintings.poem:
a small church
sent a small gift
by a tired messenger.

heaven smelled it
like incense.

nothing given in love
is small up there.

and so the letter ends
the way it began—
with grace,

left on the table
for all of you,
like bread
still warm.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Read the closing words aloud in the stillness: “and so the letter ends the way it began— with grace, left on the table for all of you, like bread still warm.” What part of your heart feels most searched or comforted by Philippians 4:18–23 right now?
